source.id: TITLE:Understanding the difficulty of training deep feedforward neural networks
source.title: Understanding the difficulty of training deep feedforward neural networks

record.file_problem: The supplied text appears to contain the full paper. No garbling or cutoff is evident.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly compares random weight initialization schemes and activation functions during gradient-based training, measuring training progress and final test error. It is an original source for the initialization claim in V4.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test-error curves and final test errors, not training classification error. It does not test V1, V2, V3, V5 or V6. It studies networks up to five hidden layers, not very deep networks or 10,000-layer convolutional networks.
record.test_reason: An original source for V4: the study compares initialization schemes and activation functions, reports convergence curves, and measures signal and gradient propagation. The extracted final-test-error rows omit its direct evidence about learning speed.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that small-random-weight sigmoid networks have poor learning dynamics, normalized initialization substantially accelerates tanh convergence, and softsign is more robust to initialization. They interpret improved signal and gradient propagation as helpful while acknowledging that several observed dynamics remain unexplained.
record.recipe_differences: Uses stochastic back-propagation with random initialization and compares a normalized initialization against a standard one; investigates activation functions and networks up to five hidden layers rather than very deep networks.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports outcomes varying with activation function and initialization scheme; the normalized initialization is particularly helpful for tanh networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 1 reports final test errors for activation and initialization combinations on four datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation function and initialization affect final generalization performance; these endpoint measurements alone do not establish learning speed or trainable depth.

record.problems: The reported table gives final test error rather than training error. Training-progress outcomes appear in figures without recoverable numeric values in the supplied text. The experiments use networks with at most five hidden layers, limiting evidence about trainable depth.

untested.parts: Training classification error in sufficiently large convolutional networks, including corrupted or random labels and CIFAR-100.
Spurious minima and the effect of extra student neurons in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Depth degradation in batch-normalized convolutional networks, identity shortcuts, very deep plain tanh networks, and residual training without normalization.
Trainable-depth limits beyond five hidden layers; ReLU-specific initialization; orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization; very deep tanh networks and 10,000-layer convolutional networks.
Above-threshold learning rates, catapult recovery, sharpness at the stability threshold, and divergence below it.

missing.what: Convergence comparisons: the authors explicitly report slower convergence with standard sigmoid and tanh networks and faster convergence with normalized tanh initialization. Softsign is less sensitive to initialization. Record qualitative speed results; exact curve values are unavailable in the supplied text.

Signal and gradient propagation comparisons: normalized versus standard initialization gives a reported layer Jacobian ratio around 0.8 versus 0.5. Standard initialization produces diminishing back-propagated gradients at initialization; normalized initialization avoids that pattern. Gradient magnitudes across layers also remain more similar during learning with normalization.

Depth-dependent saturation under standard sigmoid initialization: the four-hidden-layer network slowly desaturates around epoch 100, whereas the five-hidden-layer model remains in the saturation regime throughout training. This is a saturation result, not a measured trainable-depth limit.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels are assigned because this study is an original source for V4. All Table 1 values match the supplied text and are percentages. The text's missing figure graphics prevent numerical reconstruction of convergence curves, but its explicit qualitative results establish that V4 is tested.

versions.untested_parts: Whether sufficiently large networks reach near-zero training classification error on CIFAR-10 or CIFAR-100, including with random or corrupted labels.
Whether extra student width avoids spurious local minima in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Whether depth degrades training and identity shortcuts prevent it; training very deep plain tanh networks; residual networks without normalization.

The study tests standard versus normalized random initialization and activation choices on networks with up to five hidden layers. It does not test initialization matched to ReLU, orthogonal weights versus Gaussian weights, or very deep plain convolutional networks.
Whether training recovers from learning rates above the stability limit or tracks the edge of stability.
Whether batch normalization speeds training or whether Fixup enables residual networks to train without normalization.
